html: Calcium is the cell's fastest messenger because it is kept scarce. A resting cell holds about twenty thousand times less calcium in its cytosol than sits outside it, and almost as steep a gradient across the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum, so opening a channel for a moment is enough to raise the local concentration a hundredfold. This module draws that machinery for an airway epithelial cell and the three ways calcium reaches the cytosol. The first is the route a particle takes. Insoluble particles do not dissolve into a signal; they touch the cell, and the vanilloid receptor TRPV1 is activated by that contact, through residues of its pore region that the solid surface reaches directly. Coal fly ash does this strongly, diesel exhaust particles less so and crystalline silica least, while several channels that the published map draws were tested with the same material and did not respond at all. The second route is the store. Inositol trisphosphate, made when a receptor upstream activates a phospholipase, binds the receptor channel of the endoplasmic reticulum and lets the store empty into the cytosol. The third is the consequence of the second, and it is the part that turns a pulse into a sustained signal. A protein in the membrane of the store, STIM1, carries a calcium-binding hand that faces the lumen. While the store is full that hand is occupied and the protein stays put. When the store empties the hand is free, the protein gathers at the places where the two membranes come within a few tens of nanometres of each other, and there it catches the channel ORAI1 and holds it open, so calcium flows in from outside to refill what was lost. Two pumps undo all of it, one returning calcium to the store and one pushing it out of the cell, each spending ATP, and together they are why a calcium signal is an event and not a new resting state. What the cell does with the signal begins with calmodulin, a small protein with four calcium-binding hands that change its shape and expose the surface by which it recognises its targets. One of those targets is calcineurin, the only phosphatase in the cell that answers to calcium directly. Activated, it strips a block of thirteen phosphates from the transcription factor NFAT in a single concerted step, which hides the signal that would export the factor from the nucleus and uncovers the one that imports it, and the factor moves in.
